Free State Health Crisis

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Doctors working in the Free State public Health Sector say the system has bene brought to collapse through a combination of ineptitude, corruption and neglect – despite repeated complaints, cries fo

Summary:
Doctors working in the Free State public Health Sector say the system has bene brought to collapse through a combination of ineptitude, corruption and neglect – despite repeated complaints, cries for help and going the extra mile.
In a devastating indictment of Free State MEC Benny Malakoane, as well as Premier Ace Magashule, they describe what they have to put up with on a daily basis – having to run hospitals with less than the bare minimum resources and working equipment, having to work themselves into the ground with patient care being effected seriously.
In an anonymous letter they write: “We are medical doctors working in government hospitals in the Free State who believe it is our duty to inform the public of the dire conditions in the Free State Department of Health.
“Not many years ago the hospitals in the Free State were among the best in the country, known not only for the world class medical care that they provided, but also as excellent training institutions for medical students, interns and registrars. Doctors used to queue for employment in these hospitals. The decline of the Free State health system has accelerated since Ace Magashule became premier, and even more so with the appointment of Benny Malakoane as MEC for Health.”


Further information:
In an anonymous letter, whistle blowers pointed out certain aspects in the health system which they have addressed several times before - without any support or change from government. Government answered this letter, but not addressing even one of the allegations.

we will focus on the problems in the health system in the Free State in general, but zoom in on three pertinent hospitals:
Thebe Hospital in Harrismith - so important because of the number of accidents happening on the N3 between the Free State and Kwazulu-Natal. It doesn't matter to which private medical aid you belong, Thebe Hospital will be the first port of medical care - you will be taken there first to be stabilised before being transferred to any other hospital. There is only a casualty unit and attempts by dedicated trauma doctors - senior doctors who have worked there for years - to set-up a proper trauma unit have failed because of a lack of support from government.

Dihlabeng Hospital in Bethlehem: a regional hospital that serves a huge part of the eastern Free State. Currently there are only 5 medical officers running a 9-department hospital. Attempts by doctors here to get support from government have failed over and over again. In leaked letters to us, it states the point that this hospital cannot function as a 24-hour facility anymore. Interns doing their house doctor's year are putting their careers on the line in order to save patients' lives.

Pelenomi Hospital in Bloemfontein - provincial hospital, once the pride and joy of the Free State Health care system. It is a training hospital for medical students of the University of the Free State. Surgeons here want to stay, because they care for their patients and the greater good of the community, but they do walk in the end. Without equipment, resources and support one can really only do so much. Theatres without air condition may sound normal, but the consequences is dire - it increases the infection rate of a patient being operated on with 25%. There aren't lights in theatres, the boilers have been broken for years, meaning no hot water, BUT also that no equipment can be sterilised at the hospital - it has to be send to another hospital. Patients lie there for weeks, waiting to be operated.

These are some of the concerns doctors have:

1. MANY HOSPITAL BUILDINGS IN A STATE OF DISREPAIR
2. CONSTANT SHORTAGE OF EVEN THE MOST BASIC MEDICATIONS AND CONSUMABLES
3. DOCTORS AND NURSING STAFF ARE NOT PAID FULLY OR NOT PROMOTED
4. AMBULANCE CRISIS AND CORRUPTION
5. THE X-RAY SERVICES IN THE FREE STATE REGIONAL HOSPITALS ARE CAPPED TO TEN HOURS OVERTIME
6. HOSPITALS IN CRISIS
7. DOCTORS NOT EMPLOYED, BUT UNNESSARY MANAGEMENT POSITION CREATED

The Free State Health Department is R800 million in the red. The department owes R 600 million in malpractice suits, which Premier Ace Magashule blames on doctors. But there are many examples of wastage.

• Once a month a gastro-enterologist is, in the name of ‘outreach’, flown from Bloemfontein, by the Emergency Medical helicopter, to a Regional Hospital, where he spends about one hour, giving a short lecture and performing at the most 2 scopes (which is usually being done by the general surgeon in any case, but in far larger numbers and far more efficiently) if the scope isn’t broken. The same is done with a child psychologist.
• The FS Health Department created a Chief Operating Officer (COO) post. According to Mondli Mvambi this was done to add further to the expertise of management, which already consisted of an MEC, Head of Department and a Deputy-Director General. Dr. Balekile Edward Mzangwa, Mayor of Maluti –a -Phofung and Thabo Mofutsanyane over the past 14 years, lacking recent experience in medicine, was appointed into this position. The COO position duplicates the work of the HOD. He also earns the same substantial salary as the HOD. He has been put in charge of regional hospitals in the Free State.
• The dire situation at Dihlabeng Hospital, such as the critical lack of doctors and equipment, as well as the broken elevators, was communicated to Mzwanga on various occasions. After receiving absolutely no feedback, plans or support from him, he was once again approached in desperation by the doctors for some guidance as to the way forward. He could not be reached as he had joined premier Ace Magashule on a trip to Cuba that included an entourage of 72 people at a cost of at least R14 million. The HOD, dr David Motau, was in Germany and could also not be reached. No one in top manageent was available to take care of the crisis.
• According to Mvambi he was there to recruit scarce skilled professionals like engineers and doctors for the Free State in order to bring about a radical improvement in the province. Yet, since the beginning of 2014, nine applicants for medical officer posts in Dihlabeng Hospital went unappointed either due to lack of funding or because the HOD didn’t find time to sign the applications. Ons 28 November, Dr. Mzwanga sat in the office of the acting CEO vowing to do his best to find doctors for the hospital as a matter of urgency. Recently a handful of applications by doctors and other medical staff were returned to Dihlabeng from head office, all unsigned. Among those were 2 applications from doctors which sat on Dr Mzwanga’s desk, untouched, since October 2014. Needless to say, these doctors found employment elsewhere.

TAC On 9 July 2014, over 100 community health workers, who had been dismissed without any explanation, and TAC activists from across the province started a peaceful vigil outside Bophelo House, in an effort to draw attention to their plight. The next day police officers, sent by Malakoane, moved in and started arresting them for an illegal gathering and had to spend an entire day in holding cells. The next day they had to appear in court and were told to appear again on 1 September 2014. The case is still dragging on. During the same period Malakoeane ordered, against hospital policy and the opinion of the consultant on call, that an ANC official and pal of his should be admitted to ICU. When news of this became public he did what he does best; he lied by denying everything. The TAC laid charges against him concerning this matter. Following a fact-finding mission across the Free State Province, where they found Free State Health in dire straits, they made some demands, including that MEC for Health, Benny Malakoane must be removed from his post.

Bethlehem

Press Release:


Free State health care
Marred by corruption, ineptitude and mismanagement, the Free State public health care sector is on the brink of collapse. Desperate doctors make do with absolutely bare minimum resources, while patients suffer the tragic consequences of the systemic failure. Despite repeated complaints, government has done little to ease their plight. Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


FREE STATE HEALTH CRISIS 1

PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

HENDRIK VAN HEERDEN: I’ve asked so many many timers please help her a nd they didn’t listen.

With only a broken leg Kathleen van Heerden went to Pelenomi Hospital in Bloemfontein just after Christmas. She never left.
She died in the arms of her eldest son, Hendrik, on Thursday morning.

HENDRIK VAN HEERDEN: Since my mother were admitted at the orthopaedic ward, the window was broken. I told them to fix the window, the patients couldn’t lay there. They don’t listen, all they they do is fix the window with a carton-box. Tuesday when I went there, the carton box was out. I told them my mother was going to die from a lung infection. When I came to the hospital, my mother was “roggling” and I saw my mother die.

Hendrik’s mom’s official death notification indicates the immediate cause of death was pulmonary aspiration, and the underlying cause? Lower respiratory tract infection. Wound sepsis is listed as another significant condition contributing to her death.

According to our Constitution, all South Africans have the right “to have access to health care services” and “a health environment that is not harmful to their health or wellbeing”.

“DR ADRIAN”: If we haven’t got the right equipment and the right medicine to do proper care where does our responsibility end?

“DR ELIZE’: I think we still try our best with what we have available and we can’t do more than that.

DR. BRYCE WICKAM: You appease your conscience by thinking you have your best in the circumstances and so you learn to live with yourself like that.

For years now, the Free State Department of Health has faced an onslaught of negative publicity - on the brink of collapse and shuffling debts in a cash-strapped system.
More importantly, patients die - or feel they don’t get the care they deserve.

HENDRIK VAN HEERDEN: I pray for nobody to go there.

Last year community health activists demanded the “immediate dismissal” of Free State Health MEC, Benny Malakoane.

In July last year, we set off to the Free State to find out what was going on.
Eight months later it seems that the situation is far more critical.

Our first stop was the Thebe District Hospital in Harrismith. This is a vital hospital for victims of road accidents on the N3 and N5 highways.

DR. BRYCE WICKAM: In my opinion, they are severely under-equipped and understaffed and under-trained to cater for the acutely injured trauma patient.

General practitioner, Dr. Bryce Wickam worked at Thebe Hospital as a senior medical officer for three years before he resigned last year.

DR. BRYCE WICKAM: The working environment was more and more and more bush medicine, it was out of my hands as to what level of care I could give.

An hour’s drive from Harrismith is the Dihlabeng Regional Hospital in Bethlehem.

DEVI LINK: The Dithlabeng Hospital in Bethlehem has a 140 beds. It doesn’t sound like a lot, but this hospital is very significant in this area. Yet, it’s run by only five doctors.

“DR ELIZE”: We’ve all gotten used to not having stuff, or making excuses or cancelling operations.

“DR ADRIAN”: People are less eager to come here to work - and to get training and now we’ve absolutely hit rock bottom.

“DR ELIZE”: My wake up call came when I stood next to a patient that was critically ill and I needed basic things. Some things as basic as an ECG and a chest x-ray and I didn’t have access to that. But when I stood there and I looked at him, I realised he might actually die. It just hit me to know that nobody cares, government doesn’t care about him and they don’t care about me.

From Bethlehem we went to Pelenomi Hospital in Bloemfontein.

DEVI LINK: Insiders here at Pelenomi Hospital said the conditions have deteriorated over the past few years, negatively affecting patient care.

DR JOHN”: The airconditioning has been broken, sometimes the theatre temperatures goes up to 30 degrees, it’s impossible to work… you’re dripping sweat in the wounds of the patients.

DR BENNY MALAKOANE/FS MEC HEALTH: Patient care and the patient safety is our number one priority.

Despite Free State Health MEC, Benny Malakoane’s confidence in his department, they started the financial year with an accrued debt of R700-million

It’s the patients who are paying the price.
Hendrik’s mom lay in Pelenomi for a month before she was operated on. By then, the wound to her leg was severely infected.

HENDRIK VAN HEERDEN: Everytime they got an excuse, your mother is first on the list, and then afterwards, they say: emergency before her, she must lie.

“DR JOHN”: There are some disciplines like for instance orthopaedic surgery where they are sort of semi-emergencies and these cases will then be admitted, because they need an operation, but they will wait.

The MEC has some answering to do. Not surprisingly, he again declined our interview request. So, we just pitched up at a press conference in Bloemfontein.

DEVI: Are you proud of the state of health in this province?

DR BENNY MALAKOANE: I am proud of myself. I am a team worker, I work within a team. I know my work and I do it well. No one needs to tell me that, no one needs to blow my horn for me, I will do it myself.

We were surprised to be met with such candour. Especially, considering that it seems as if the department missed some strategic 2014-goals - such as having a 95% availibity of essential drugs. A target the MEC boasted they did reach.

[SABC 6 JULY 2014] DR BENNY MALAKOANE: Our drug stocks in terms of antibiotics and other life-prolonging medicine are more than 95% in all of our facilities.

But the Stop-Stockouts Project, disproved this through a 2013 national survey. Fifty-four percent of the province’s facilities were out of stock or short of ARV and/or TB medicine.
A 2014 snap-survey indicated there was no improvement.

“DR ELIZE”: You’re always out of something. The question is basically just what’s going next?

DR. BRYCE WICKAM: we ran out of spinal injection which we use to give anaesthesia for spinal for C-sections, which we do a lot of this hospital and we were just told we must make up our own one. So it would be, the critical component is you need sugar in this solution, so we draw up sugar from a separate drip and we just make our own mixture, which is unacceptable

DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: When you are saying they are making concoc… their own concoctions to make spinal…that doesn’t happen here.

DR. BRYCE WICKAM: It was senior management. When we confronted senior management, we were told that we should make our own.
DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: I will investigate that, they will tell who told them to do wrong things.

It’s inconceivable that hospitals have to function without basic medical consumables like the right sized gloves, syringes and needles.

“DR ELIZE”: The big crisis at the moment is colostomy bags. We have actually heard horror stories of patients who use shopping bags that they tape around the colostomy.

“DR JOHN”: You have to improvise; you are transgressing very serious and strict rules when it comes to patients’ safety.

In the orthopaedic department at Pelenomi, insiders claim only two drill sets are working.

“DR JOHN”: I’m told that doctors even had to put the pins in by hand. They have to open up the canal of the femur manually. It is usually done with power equipment.

But it’s not only the lack of medcine, consumables and functional equipment that challenge medical professionals. At Dihlabeng we found this notice on the lifts.

DEVI: So what did you do? The elevators did not work at your hospital?

DR ADRIAN: Corpses had to be carried downstairs to the mortuary in body bags in full view of - visitors and other patients.

Insiders claim that operations and even simple procedures at Pelenomi are often delayed for at least six weeks.

“DR JOHN”: There are a couple of factors that cause the delays in theatre: the anaesthetic equipment, and then there just a complete overflow of patients. Theatre lights frequently are a problem, so sometimes you work with like, half of the theatre lights. If they are completely out, you can’t operate.

DEVI: Let’s look at Pelenomi Hospital: problem with anaesthesia machines, theatre lights not working, patients lying around with broken arms and broken legs, but they can’t have operations within the next six to eight weeks?

DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: I am sure you heard horrifying stories. But you know, sometimes what need to happen, when people say lights are not working, just do yourself a favour, switch on the plug and see if the lights go on or not.

Pictures leaked to us, all taken this week show the right-hand light is dim and flickers. When the two lights touch, there is a short circuit and one switches off.

DEVI: You are saying this is nonsense?

DR. BENNY MOLAKOANE: All that you are saying is sensation. I think they are abusing it. Health is an emotive issue.

DEVI: How often do you walk into theatre and you are not dealing with the full pack here.

“DR JOHN”: I would say about 85% of the time.

Free State Health’s financial statements for 2013/14 indicate that out of a budget of 7,89-billion, only 11,3% was spent on medical supplies and medcine. That is 896 million.
Compared to the amount of R4,5-billion spent on employees’ salaries and wages, it doesn’t seem to add up.

The doctors at Dihlabeng say they have tried in vain to make MEC Malakoane realise the urgency of the situation. Letters leaked to us indicate they had officially asked for his intervention in 2013 and 2015, saying it’s impossible to run a 24-hour service with so few medical officers.

“DR ELIZE”: We lost a lot of doctors in the past few months. We had a lot of doctors who’ve been working extra hours - they were paid for the extra hours they’d put in, but I think a lot of them did not for the financial gain - but basically for just trying to keep the services running.

DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: The kind of overtime for example that is being paid by this department, it is just too exorbitant for us to tolerate and in my term of office, I will not allow that to happen and I will force people to comply and do things the way I would like them to be done.

“DR ELIZE”: Last year we had a few doctors who did a lot more than what they should have, more than what they or anyone can handle, and of those doctors one is left. At some stage you just realise there is no use fighting the system.

DR BENNY MALAKOANE: Someone else who is either disgruntled or unhappy, who may have been a beneficiary of this kind of rot decides to choose the media as a means to complain. I am driven by negativity, it makes me perform better.

DR BRYCE WICKAM: 41:15 Come and spend a day in our shoes, come and work alongside us without the whooha, just come and work with us, maybe they don’t know, maybe they only see what is on paper, I don’t know. But what I do know is that if they saw what we saw, they would want change as much as we do.

Piatt UCM1025_001 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 22 March 2015 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 25 March 2015 Press Release: Free State health care Marred by corruption, ineptitude and mismanagement, the Free State public health care sector is on the brink of collapse. Desperate doctors make do with absolutely bare minimum resources, while patients suffer the tragic consequences of the systemic failure. Despite repeated complaints, government has done little to ease their plight. Carte Blanche investigates. Script: FREE STATE HEALTH CRISIS 1 PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK HENDRIK VAN HEERDEN: I’ve asked so many many timers please help her a nd they didn’t listen. With only a broken leg Kathleen van Heerden went to Pelenomi Hospital in Bloemfontein just after Christmas. She never left. She died in the arms of her eldest son, Hendrik, on Thursday morning. HENDRIK VAN HEERDEN: Since my mother were admitted at the orthopaedic ward, the window was broken. I told them to fix the window, the patients couldn’t lay there. They don’t listen, all they they do is fix the window with a carton-box. Tuesday when I went there, the carton box was out. I told them my mother was going to die from a lung infection. When I came to the hospital, my mother was “roggling” and I saw my mother die. Hendrik’s mom’s official death notification indicates the immediate cause of death was pulmonary aspiration, and the underlying cause? Lower respiratory tract infection. Wound sepsis is listed as another significant condition contributing to her death. According to our Constitution, all South Africans have the right “to have access to health care services” and “a health environment that is not harmful to their health or wellbeing”. “DR ADRIAN”: If we haven’t got the right equipment and the right medicine to do proper care where does our responsibility end? “DR ELIZE’: I think we still try our best with what we have available and we can’t do more than that. DR. BRYCE WICKAM: You appease your conscience by thinking you have your best in the circumstances and so you learn to live with yourself like that. For years now, the Free State Department of Health has faced an onslaught of negative publicity - on the brink of collapse and shuffling debts in a cash-strapped system. More importantly, patients die - or feel they don’t get the care they deserve. HENDRIK VAN HEERDEN: I pray for nobody to go there. Last year community health activists demanded the “immediate dismissal” of Free State Health MEC, Benny Malakoane. In July last year, we set off to the Free State to find out what was going on. Eight months later it seems that the situation is far more critical. Our first stop was the Thebe District Hospital in Harrismith. This is a vital hospital for victims of road accidents on the N3 and N5 highways. DR. BRYCE WICKAM: In my opinion, they are severely under-equipped and understaffed and under-trained to cater for the acutely injured trauma patient. General practitioner, Dr. Bryce Wickam worked at Thebe Hospital as a senior medical officer for three years before he resigned last year. DR. BRYCE WICKAM: The working environment was more and more and more bush medicine, it was out of my hands as to what level of care I could give. An hour’s drive from Harrismith is the Dihlabeng Regional Hospital in Bethlehem. DEVI LINK: The Dithlabeng Hospital in Bethlehem has a 140 beds. It doesn’t sound like a lot, but this hospital is very significant in this area. Yet, it’s run by only five doctors. “DR ELIZE”: We’ve all gotten used to not having stuff, or making excuses or cancelling operations. “DR ADRIAN”: People are less eager to come here to work - and to get training and now we’ve absolutely hit rock bottom. “DR ELIZE”: My wake up call came when I stood next to a patient that was critically ill and I needed basic things. Some things as basic as an ECG and a chest x-ray and I didn’t have access to that. But when I stood there and I looked at him, I realised he might actually die. It just hit me to know that nobody cares, government doesn’t care about him and they don’t care about me. From Bethlehem we went to Pelenomi Hospital in Bloemfontein. DEVI LINK: Insiders here at Pelenomi Hospital said the conditions have deteriorated over the past few years, negatively affecting patient care. DR JOHN”: The airconditioning has been broken, sometimes the theatre temperatures goes up to 30 degrees, it’s impossible to work… you’re dripping sweat in the wounds of the patients. DR BENNY MALAKOANE/FS MEC HEALTH: Patient care and the patient safety is our number one priority. Despite Free State Health MEC, Benny Malakoane’s confidence in his department, they started the financial year with an accrued debt of R700-million It’s the patients who are paying the price. Hendrik’s mom lay in Pelenomi for a month before she was operated on. By then, the wound to her leg was severely infected. HENDRIK VAN HEERDEN: Everytime they got an excuse, your mother is first on the list, and then afterwards, they say: emergency before her, she must lie. “DR JOHN”: There are some disciplines like for instance orthopaedic surgery where they are sort of semi-emergencies and these cases will then be admitted, because they need an operation, but they will wait. The MEC has some answering to do. Not surprisingly, he again declined our interview request. So, we just pitched up at a press conference in Bloemfontein. DEVI: Are you proud of the state of health in this province? DR BENNY MALAKOANE: I am proud of myself. I am a team worker, I work within a team. I know my work and I do it well. No one needs to tell me that, no one needs to blow my horn for me, I will do it myself. We were surprised to be met with such candour. Especially, considering that it seems as if the department missed some strategic 2014-goals - such as having a 95% availibity of essential drugs. A target the MEC boasted they did reach. [SABC 6 JULY 2014] DR BENNY MALAKOANE: Our drug stocks in terms of antibiotics and other life-prolonging medicine are more than 95% in all of our facilities. But the Stop-Stockouts Project, disproved this through a 2013 national survey. Fifty-four percent of the province’s facilities were out of stock or short of ARV and/or TB medicine. A 2014 snap-survey indicated there was no improvement. “DR ELIZE”: You’re always out of something. The question is basically just what’s going next? DR. BRYCE WICKAM: we ran out of spinal injection which we use to give anaesthesia for spinal for C-sections, which we do a lot of this hospital and we were just told we must make up our own one. So it would be, the critical component is you need sugar in this solution, so we draw up sugar from a separate drip and we just make our own mixture, which is unacceptable DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: When you are saying they are making concoc… their own concoctions to make spinal…that doesn’t happen here. DR. BRYCE WICKAM: It was senior management. When we confronted senior management, we were told that we should make our own. DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: I will investigate that, they will tell who told them to do wrong things. It’s inconceivable that hospitals have to function without basic medical consumables like the right sized gloves, syringes and needles. “DR ELIZE”: The big crisis at the moment is colostomy bags. We have actually heard horror stories of patients who use shopping bags that they tape around the colostomy. “DR JOHN”: You have to improvise; you are transgressing very serious and strict rules when it comes to patients’ safety. In the orthopaedic department at Pelenomi, insiders claim only two drill sets are working. “DR JOHN”: I’m told that doctors even had to put the pins in by hand. They have to open up the canal of the femur manually. It is usually done with power equipment. But it’s not only the lack of medcine, consumables and functional equipment that challenge medical professionals. At Dihlabeng we found this notice on the lifts. DEVI: So what did you do? The elevators did not work at your hospital? DR ADRIAN: Corpses had to be carried downstairs to the mortuary in body bags in full view of - visitors and other patients. Insiders claim that operations and even simple procedures at Pelenomi are often delayed for at least six weeks. “DR JOHN”: There are a couple of factors that cause the delays in theatre: the anaesthetic equipment, and then there just a complete overflow of patients. Theatre lights frequently are a problem, so sometimes you work with like, half of the theatre lights. If they are completely out, you can’t operate. DEVI: Let’s look at Pelenomi Hospital: problem with anaesthesia machines, theatre lights not working, patients lying around with broken arms and broken legs, but they can’t have operations within the next six to eight weeks? DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: I am sure you heard horrifying stories. But you know, sometimes what need to happen, when people say lights are not working, just do yourself a favour, switch on the plug and see if the lights go on or not. Pictures leaked to us, all taken this week show the right-hand light is dim and flickers. When the two lights touch, there is a short circuit and one switches off. DEVI: You are saying this is nonsense? DR. BENNY MOLAKOANE: All that you are saying is sensation. I think they are abusing it. Health is an emotive issue. DEVI: How often do you walk into theatre and you are not dealing with the full pack here. “DR JOHN”: I would say about 85% of the time. Free State Health’s financial statements for 2013/14 indicate that out of a budget of 7,89-billion, only 11,3% was spent on medical supplies and medcine. That is 896 million. Compared to the amount of R4,5-billion spent on employees’ salaries and wages, it doesn’t seem to add up. The doctors at Dihlabeng say they have tried in vain to make MEC Malakoane realise the urgency of the situation. Letters leaked to us indicate they had officially asked for his intervention in 2013 and 2015, saying it’s impossible to run a 24-hour service with so few medical officers. “DR ELIZE”: We lost a lot of doctors in the past few months. We had a lot of doctors who’ve been working extra hours - they were paid for the extra hours they’d put in, but I think a lot of them did not for the financial gain - but basically for just trying to keep the services running. DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: The kind of overtime for example that is being paid by this department, it is just too exorbitant for us to tolerate and in my term of office, I will not allow that to happen and I will force people to comply and do things the way I would like them to be done. “DR ELIZE”: Last year we had a few doctors who did a lot more than what they should have, more than what they or anyone can handle, and of those doctors one is left. At some stage you just realise there is no use fighting the system. DR BENNY MALAKOANE: Someone else who is either disgruntled or unhappy, who may have been a beneficiary of this kind of rot decides to choose the media as a means to complain. I am driven by negativity, it makes me perform better. DR BRYCE WICKAM: 41:15 Come and spend a day in our shoes, come and work alongside us without the whooha, just come and work with us, maybe they don’t know, maybe they only see what is on paper, I don’t know. But what I do know is that if they saw what we saw, they would want change as much as we do.

metadata.Summary: Doctors working in the Free State public Health Sector say the system has bene brought to collapse through a combination of ineptitude, corruption and neglect – despite repeated complaints, cries for help and going the extra mile. In a devastating indictment of Free State MEC Benny Malakoane, as well as Premier Ace Magashule, they describe what they have to put up with on a daily basis – having to run hospitals with less than the bare minimum resources and working equipment, having to work themselves into the ground with patient care being effected seriously. In an anonymous letter they write: “We are medical doctors working in government hospitals in the Free State who believe it is our duty to inform the public of the dire conditions in the Free State Department of Health. “Not many years ago the hospitals in the Free State were among the best in the country, known not only for the world class medical care that they provided, but also as excellent training institutions for medical students, interns and registrars. Doctors used to queue for employment in these hospitals. The decline of the Free State health system has accelerated since Ace Magashule became premier, and even more so with the appointment of Benny Malakoane as MEC for Health.”
metadata.Further information: In an anonymous letter, whistle blowers pointed out certain aspects in the health system which they have addressed several times before - without any support or change from government. Government answered this letter, but not addressing even one of the allegations. we will focus on the problems in the health system in the Free State in general, but zoom in on three pertinent hospitals: Thebe Hospital in Harrismith - so important because of the number of accidents happening on the N3 between the Free State and Kwazulu-Natal. It doesn't matter to which private medical aid you belong, Thebe Hospital will be the first port of medical care - you will be taken there first to be stabilised before being transferred to any other hospital. There is only a casualty unit and attempts by dedicated trauma doctors - senior doctors who have worked there for years - to set-up a proper trauma unit have failed because of a lack of support from government. Dihlabeng Hospital in Bethlehem: a regional hospital that serves a huge part of the eastern Free State. Currently there are only 5 medical officers running a 9-department hospital. Attempts by doctors here to get support from government have failed over and over again. In leaked letters to us, it states the point that this hospital cannot function as a 24-hour facility anymore. Interns doing their house doctor's year are putting their careers on the line in order to save patients' lives. Pelenomi Hospital in Bloemfontein - provincial hospital, once the pride and joy of the Free State Health care system. It is a training hospital for medical students of the University of the Free State. Surgeons here want to stay, because they care for their patients and the greater good of the community, but they do walk in the end. Without equipment, resources and support one can really only do so much. Theatres without air condition may sound normal, but the consequences is dire - it increases the infection rate of a patient being operated on with 25%. There aren't lights in theatres, the boilers have been broken for years, meaning no hot water, BUT also that no equipment can be sterilised at the hospital - it has to be send to another hospital. Patients lie there for weeks, waiting to be operated. These are some of the concerns doctors have: 1. MANY HOSPITAL BUILDINGS IN A STATE OF DISREPAIR 2. CONSTANT SHORTAGE OF EVEN THE MOST BASIC MEDICATIONS AND CONSUMABLES 3. DOCTORS AND NURSING STAFF ARE NOT PAID FULLY OR NOT PROMOTED 4. AMBULANCE CRISIS AND CORRUPTION 5. THE X-RAY SERVICES IN THE FREE STATE REGIONAL HOSPITALS ARE CAPPED TO TEN HOURS OVERTIME 6. HOSPITALS IN CRISIS 7. DOCTORS NOT EMPLOYED, BUT UNNESSARY MANAGEMENT POSITION CREATED The Free State Health Department is R800 million in the red. The department owes R 600 million in malpractice suits, which Premier Ace Magashule blames on doctors. But there are many examples of wastage. • Once a month a gastro-enterologist is, in the name of ‘outreach’, flown from Bloemfontein, by the Emergency Medical helicopter, to a Regional Hospital, where he spends about one hour, giving a short lecture and performing at the most 2 scopes (which is usually being done by the general surgeon in any case, but in far larger numbers and far more efficiently) if the scope isn’t broken. The same is done with a child psychologist. • The FS Health Department created a Chief Operating Officer (COO) post. According to Mondli Mvambi this was done to add further to the expertise of management, which already consisted of an MEC, Head of Department and a Deputy-Director General. Dr. Balekile Edward Mzangwa, Mayor of Maluti –a -Phofung and Thabo Mofutsanyane over the past 14 years, lacking recent experience in medicine, was appointed into this position. The COO position duplicates the work of the HOD. He also earns the same substantial salary as the HOD. He has been put in charge of regional hospitals in the Free State. • The dire situation at Dihlabeng Hospital, such as the critical lack of doctors and equipment, as well as the broken elevators, was communicated to Mzwanga on various occasions. After receiving absolutely no feedback, plans or support from him, he was once again approached in desperation by the doctors for some guidance as to the way forward. He could not be reached as he had joined premier Ace Magashule on a trip to Cuba that included an entourage of 72 people at a cost of at least R14 million. The HOD, dr David Motau, was in Germany and could also not be reached. No one in top manageent was available to take care of the crisis. • According to Mvambi he was there to recruit scarce skilled professionals like engineers and doctors for the Free State in order to bring about a radical improvement in the province. Yet, since the beginning of 2014, nine applicants for medical officer posts in Dihlabeng Hospital went unappointed either due to lack of funding or because the HOD didn’t find time to sign the applications. Ons 28 November, Dr. Mzwanga sat in the office of the acting CEO vowing to do his best to find doctors for the hospital as a matter of urgency. Recently a handful of applications by doctors and other medical staff were returned to Dihlabeng from head office, all unsigned. Among those were 2 applications from doctors which sat on Dr Mzwanga’s desk, untouched, since October 2014. Needless to say, these doctors found employment elsewhere. TAC On 9 July 2014, over 100 community health workers, who had been dismissed without any explanation, and TAC activists from across the province started a peaceful vigil outside Bophelo House, in an effort to draw attention to their plight. The next day police officers, sent by Malakoane, moved in and started arresting them for an illegal gathering and had to spend an entire day in holding cells. The next day they had to appear in court and were told to appear again on 1 September 2014. The case is still dragging on. During the same period Malakoeane ordered, against hospital policy and the opinion of the consultant on call, that an ANC official and pal of his should be admitted to ICU. When news of this became public he did what he does best; he lied by denying everything. The TAC laid charges against him concerning this matter. Following a fact-finding mission across the Free State Province, where they found Free State Health in dire straits, they made some demands, including that MEC for Health, Benny Malakoane must be removed from his post.
